book_title: Across the Nala: A Queer Dalit Bahujan Zine of Stories from Delhi
subject_line: The Sahibi river and what counts as a nala
email_body:
Dear Dhiren,

In launching Across the Nala, you pointed out that the Sahibi river is not marked as a nala on maps, even though that is effectively what it has become. That gap between the official map and the lived one runs through the ten stories, some literally set across the water, others using it as a figure for caste history. I would love to ask how the storytelling and zine-making workshop shaped which version of Delhi ended up on the page.

book_title: We Were Always Eating Expired Things
subject_line: The prose poems behind We Were Always Eating Expired Things
email_body:
Dear Cheryl,

In your Ploughshares interview about We Were Always Eating Expired Things, you said the prose poems were written as a single piece and then broken up, so that their narrative sits behind the whole collection. You also described trying to fashion a vocabulary of loneliness. Ten years after the Singapore Literature Prize shortlist, I would be curious how that vocabulary has carried into your teaching and newer writing, and whether the splitting-up method still shapes how you build a sequence.

subject_line: Crooked River, Atikokan and the summers behind Hummingbird
email_body:
Dear Tristan,

Hummingbird moves the reader a long way from the Anglesey of Send My Cold Bones Home and Revenant, to a lake in northern Ontario and a fictional Crooked River modelled on Atikokan, where you spent childhood summers. Zachary Tayler's isolated life with his father there won the Edward Stanford Award for fiction with a sense of place. I would like to ask how writing a second home, rather than the island, changed the way you handle landscape on the page.

subject_line: The burning house at the start of How to Carry Fire
email_body:
Dear Christina,

How to Carry Fire opens with the burning of your childhood home, and the fire then keeps changing shape across the collection, from destruction to warmth to something like renewal, moving between American and Welsh landscapes. After More Than You Were dealt with your father's addiction and death, I am curious what it meant to come back to that family history through a single image, and how you decided the title poem's way of holding fire without being consumed by it.

subject_line: Christopher by day, Alexander by night in Equinox
email_body:
Dear David,

In Equinox, the witch hunter Christopher Morden shares one body with Alexander, a musician who takes over at night, and the investigation into a mutilated woman ends up splitting the two of them over a witch Alexander wants to save. Reviewers have called it fantasy noir and a supernatural detective story at once. I would like to ask how you managed the practical side of writing two people who never meet yet keep negotiating the same life.

subject_line: A ghost in a martini, from Wisconsin to Swansea
email_body:
Dear Alan,

You, Me and the Birds has a ghost in a martini and a lover reimagined as a listed building, and it lets Wisconsin and Wales run into each other, alongside Tony Goble's paintings. Since you came to Swansea from the American Midwest and now also edit poetry for Parthian, I would like to ask how that double vantage point has shifted since the debut, and what editing other poets has changed in how you finish your own poems.

subject_line: One solstice day with the Avens family
email_body:
Dear Elizabeth,

An Archive of Happiness keeps the whole novel inside a single day, the Avens family's annual gathering in the Highlands at the summer solstice, and lets what happens there force a fractured family to redraw its bonds. From Ramshackle onward, setting seems to do a lot of the holding together in your fiction. I would like to ask why one day felt like the right container, and what the structure let you do with loss and repair.

subject_line: Bubbles, surfaces and You Name It
email_body:
Dear Colin,

In your SPAM interview you described You Name It as a book about bubbles, and reading that next to Steven Waling's sense that Click + Collect was about surfaces, I sense a long interest in what floats on top and what gives way, carried through Swamp Kiss and Aquafaba with real playfulness. I would like to ask how that lightness and attention to surfaces works for you as a way into serious material, and where it has taken you since.

subject_line: From Uncle's Singlish to Becoming an HDB Flat
email_body:
Dear Ann,

Many readers first met you through Uncle and the Singlish-English stories of Bang My Car, so it was striking to move to Burning Walls for Paper Spirits, with its free verse, Chelsea Sia's illustrations, and poems such as "Becoming an HDB Flat" that place a public housing block alongside someone the speaker is close to. I would like to ask how moving from Uncle's voice to these quieter, more tactile poems changed what you listen for in Singapore's everyday spaces.
